# Document Purpose

### Propose a successor to UKMARSBOT

This document is intended to highlight the changes and new design requirements for the version 2 of the UKMARSBOT. This only focuses on the hardware requirements for the robot and will point out differences between the new design and the currently available v1 design.

### Reduce barriers to entry

This new version is intended to reduce the barrier of entry to new members / competitors / students in half size line following, wall following and classic maze solving competitions. This new robot will be unsuitable for half size maze solving.

### Provide a design more suited to use in schools

The secondary purpose of this project to help create a path for educators in introducing children to the world of programming, microcontrollers, electronics and robotics. Education appears to prefer the Python programming language when teaching students, and newcomers to programming appear to start with Python as well. While there are many microcontrollers that will run MicroPython or CircuitPython, schools in the UK have widely adopted the RP2040 device running MicroPython.

RP2040 is designed by the Raspberry Pi foundation, who have a huge focus in creating cheap computing for education. Therefore, having a solution that is able to use a Raspberry Pi controller has potential for additional benefits in terms of advertising, budgets and appeal.

# Competition

There are already many microcontroller robots that can be bought off the shelf. These appear to be designed to cover off the educational aspect of our project and for one reason or another do not work for our purposes. They are either too big for a maze or the sensors are too slow or not configured for our events.

It is important that we don’t end up creating a clone of something that already exists. For example:

- The picoBot - <https://shop.4tronix.co.uk/products/bitbotpro>
- Another pico robot - <https://kitronik.co.uk/products/5335-autonomous-robotics-platform-for-pico>

There are several available “development” boards like the <https://shop.pimoroni.com/products/inventor-2040-w?variant=40053063155795> that have a lot of if not all the required features to build a robot but these are still unsuitable for our specific competition examples. Their unsuitability is related to the boards physical size and lack of mounting points for motors and sensors.

# High Level design choices

- Stick with the physical layout of the UKMARSBOT v1.x PCB. Now referred to as the chassis board.
- Sticking with through hole design
  - A version 2.5 will be investigated to see if the whole chassis board, sensor boards and components could be manufactured by a PCB supplier at a later date.
- Make the chassis board microcontroller agnostic. The chassis will handle the
  - DC motor controller
  - Battery mounting and power input
  - A 5v power rail
  - A microcontroller power rail, likely to be 3.3v from an RP2040
  - Power switch
  - At least one function button
  - Motor mounting
  - Wiring for both motors and encoders
  - Socket and mounting for plugging in a microcontroller adaptor board
  - Socket and mounting for sensor boards
- Microcontrollers will be mounted to an intermediate “mezzanine” adaptor board. These boards will allow for any number of microcontrollers to be used without effecting the chassis or sensor boards.
- Update the sensor boards designs to ensure options exists for 3 ADC inputs and due to the 3.3v limit of the RP2040 chips create 2 power rails for sensor boards. A 5v rail for powering emitters (LED’s) and a “microcontroller” rail (3.3v or 5v) to power the receivers (photo transistors)
- Bluetooth to be handled by the microcontroller or the end user

# What we aren’t building

- A super-fast plug and play competition winning robot
  - The focus should be on starting people from zero and getting to course complete. Showing them a path of how to get faster
- A generic motor / sensor control board
- A slightly different version of an existing off the shelf product

This section goes through all of the various option for each section of hardware that is needed for a mouse.

## Concept Images

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 1 - CAD concept of UKMARSBOT v2

## Chassis Board

The current UKMARSBOT main board shape and dimensions are maintained. This is already a proven platform size and can successfully compete in the required competitions.

The chassis will need to handle the following:

- DC motor controller mounting
- Battery mounting and power input
- A 5v power rail
- A microcontroller power rail, likely to be 3.3v from an RP2040
- Power switch
- At least one function button
- Motor mounting
- Wiring for both motors and encoders
- Socket and mounting for plugging in a microcontroller mezzanine board
- Socket and mounting for sensor boards

The interface between the chassis and mezzanine board will need to carry the following

- Ground
- 5v
- 3.3 / Microcontroller voltage
- GPIO for chassis button
- 4 ADC for sensors
- 3 GPIO for sensors
- 2 GPIO for Motor Direction
- 2 GPIO / PWM for Motor power
- 4 GPIO for encoders

Note: For reasons I am unable to explain. The quadrature encoder code used in micro python requires that the encoder A and B wires are used by sequential GPIO pins. I.E. 18 and 19 or 22 and 23. This will be important when designing a circuit for the motor encoders mapping to the microcontroller.

## Mezzanine Boards

The mezzanine boards size needs and height to be determined. Clearly it must sit clear of the motors but user may want it to extend rearwards over the battery as well. The idea being that people will be able to create their own mezzanine boards out of strip board or equivalent for boards we don’t yet support.

For launch we should provide 2 mezzanine boards for people to choose from

- Pico W board
- Maker Nano RP2040 board
  - This could probably be used for the Arduino nano connect. The pin layout is the same but some GPIO pins have different numbering
  - Expose pins suitable for a Bluetooth adaptor to be added

This mezzanine approach also solves the problem that educators have of requiring extra components to be available on the robot. Any extra hardware like buzzers, LED’s or Bluetooth can be added to the mezzanine board.

## Sensors

The current designs of sensor boards have been proven to work but need a subtle update to work with the new design

All 3 sensor boards need the following updates

- Update to allow for 5v rail and 3.3 (microcontroller rail)
- Emitter to use 5v
- Sensors to use microcontroller ADC voltage

The end result will be the offering of

- 3 ADC wall sensor board with 2 GPIO to toggle front and side emitters
- 3 ADC line follower sensor board
- 4 ADC wall sensor board with 2 GPIO to toggle front and side emitters

## Bluetooth and remote communication

Bluetooth communication needs to be handled by the microcontroller or via a custom addition to a mezzanine board.

## Microcontroller options

Lots of RP2040 options but the table below shows the most obvious options for a robot build

| Name | Board Dimensions | High Level Specs | Price | Comments |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Raspberry Pi Pico W | 21mm x 51.3mm x 3.9mm | 2×SPI, 2×I2C, 2×UART, 3×12-bit ADC, 16×controllable PWM channels | £5.80 | Very cheap and has Wi-Fi and Bluetooth built in.<br><br>No LED’s or extra’s<br><br>Only 3 ADC<br><br>Input Voltage – 5v |
| Raspberry Pi Pico | 21mm x 51.3mm x 3.9mm | 2×SPI, 2×I2C, 2×UART, 3×12-bit ADC, 16×controllable PWM channels | £3.80 | Mega cheap but offset with no Bluetooth. Pico W probably better option over the 2<br><br>Input Voltage – 5v |
| Maker Nano RP2040 | 49.53mm x 21.08mm | Same as pico but<br><br>14x Status indicator LEDs for GPIOs<br><br>1x Piezo buzzer with mute switch<br><br>1x Pushbutton<br><br>2x RGB LEDs (WS2812 Neopixel)<br><br>4x ADC | £9.50 | This board has 4 ADC.<br><br>Covers most of the schools peripheral requirements without the need of extra boards and components.<br><br>No build in Wi-Fi or Bluetooth<br><br>Input Voltage - 7-30V |
| Arduino Nano RP2040 Connect | 43.18 mm x 17.78mm | 14x Digital Pin<br><br>8x Analog Pin<br><br>Micro USB<br><br>UART, SPI, I2C Support | £26 | This board has 4 ADC from RP2040 and 4 ADC from NINA chip (not accessed successfully)<br><br>NINA-W102 radio module<br><br>16MB flash memory<br><br>Input Voltage – 5-21v |
|     |     |     |     |     |

An important takeaway from these options is the lack of voltage regulation on the pico boards. Meaning that the main board must be able to to convert battery voltage to a 5v supply rail.

From the above list the maker nano is probably the better choice as this has all the LED’s and buzzer the school desire, gives 4 ADC’s, takes battery voltage but does not have Bluetooth

## Motors

Motors are a somewhat easy choice. The N20 form factor is well established and easy to obtain. For our purposes they do need to have encoders. There is a debate on what gear ratio we would recommend. I suggest 1:50 as a starting point.

## Motor Controller

Peter has done a lot of work on comparing DC motor controllers. I don’t remember there being a clear winner. Performance isn’t the primary factor for this application. Simplicity and price along with easily available should win here.

A controller that only needs 4 GPIO pins should be used as these are very easy to explain how to work. 1 pin for direction control and 1 pin for power per motor.

| Name | Price | Easily available? | Comments |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| TB6612FNG | £9.66 |     | Either needs more components on the board or needs a lot of GPIO pins |
| [DFRobot TB6612FNG](https://uk.robotshop.com/products/dfrobot-tb6612fng-2x12a-dc-motor-driver-module) | £4.43 | Available on digikey but sold out on other sites | Only needs 4 GPIO pins. Easy to drive |
| [DRV8835](https://www.pololu.com/product/2135) | £5.00 |     |     |
| [TB6612FNG](https://uk.robotshop.com/products/pololu-dual-dc-motor-driver-1a-4-5v-3-5v-tb6612fng) | £4.89 | Sold out |     |
| [DRV8833](https://www.amazon.co.uk/DollaTek-DRV8833-2-Channel-Ultra-small-Voltage/dp/B07ML2RDNY) | £4.99 for 5 | Lots of versions on amazon | Only needs 4 GPIO pins. Easy to drive |

## Batteries

The simplest solution is to suggest and stick with the PP3 9v form factor. Lots of people are already using these batteries and they are fairly cheap, easy to recharge and have a long run time. This does not prevent people from upgrading or using different form factor batteries in the future.

[Example set of batteries](https://www.amazon.co.uk/EBL-Rechargeable-9V-Lithium-Batteries/dp/B089CRTDDY)

# Mouse Software

The following is a high-level list of desired software snippets or solutions. Assumed to be written in Micro python.

I have no idea who would write these and I know there is a very fine line between providing enough examples so that people can then solve a problem or giving them too much code and them not understanding what is going on

- MazeRunner-core (An alpha version of this is available)
- Simple line follower
- Simple wall follower
- Simple maze solver
- LED blink test
- Encoder test code
- Motor test code
- Sensor test code
